cells.tense: The thinking is fast right now, and you are the one holding the knife.
cells.ask: Take one open question today and reason it all the way to an answer, then say the answer out loud to someone. Don't hedge it, don't qualify it. Let it land as yours.
cells.core: You can take a tangle and cut to the thing underneath it. Not by force — by speed. The reasoning moves faster than the noise around it, and what's left when it stops is usually right.\n\nIt works because nothing is decided yet and you know that. You're not defending a position. You're holding a question open with the door still shut, thinking clearly inside it. That's why people start repeating what you say a week later. The knife is sharp because you haven't committed it to anything. Keep it that way. Keep the questions you're cutting into ones where you genuinely don't know the answer yet.
cells.sheetLine: You cut to what's true, and you haven't decided yet.
cells.verb: cutting through to what is actually true
cells.place: the open moment before anything has been decided

cells.tense: You are running the whole conversation in advance, before it has actually started.
cells.ask: Pick one unresolved thing and leave it unresolved for a full day. Don't explain it, don't defend it, don't decide it. Just let it sit, and notice what happens when nothing gets settled.
cells.core: You've already argued the whole thing out in your head before it starts. Every response anticipated, every objection answered, the conclusion reached before anyone else gets a word in. The thinking has gotten very fast at turning a live question into a solved one.\n\nThat speed is real, and it's costing you. The other person can't meet you in a conversation you've already finished. And you can't be surprised by anything, which means nothing new gets in. Here's the fix: not more analysis. The opposite. Hold something steady long enough that it doesn't need settling yet. You know how to cut. Today, try not cutting.
cells.sheetLine: You've finished the argument before anyone else starts it.

cells.tense: You started thinking clearly once, and then you stopped before you got anywhere.
cells.ask: Say one half-formed idea out loud to another person before you've worked it out. It doesn't need to be good. Watch what happens when they ask you a follow-up question about it.
cells.core: You can take a half-formed shape and follow it until it says something clean. That part still works. When it's going well, you don't need the finished version first — you say the rough thing and the rough thing turns out to be enough to start from, and the person across from you takes it somewhere you couldn't have gotten alone.\n\nWhat's happening instead is that you wait. For the right moment, the right room, the right version. Everything stays unfinished and nothing gets tested, and the sharpness you do have has nowhere to land. The thinking isn't the problem. It's that nothing leaves your head, so nothing gets a chance to get better. One conversation would do more than a month of working it out privately.
cells.sheetLine: You've stopped saying the thought before it's finished.

cells.tense: You are already cutting through things, and you are calling it something else.
cells.ask: Find one moment this week where your reasoning changed what someone did. Then say, out loud, 'that was mine.' Not 'the work needed it.' Not 'anyone would have seen it.' Just yours.
cells.core: You can hear the shape of a problem and get to what's actually underneath it. When it's going well, that shows up as a sentence in the room — the one thing somebody repeats back to you a week later. The speed is there. The sharpness is there. What runs past you is that it came from you.\n\nYou describe it as the situation, or the obvious thing, or what any reasonable person would see. That habit costs you something. Your own work stays invisible to you, so it doesn't stack into anything you can stand on. Someone shifted their position this week because of a sentence you said. You can still check whether that's true. If it is, the sentence was yours.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that this person's fast strategic thinking is a capacity they own and can direct; the record only says the pattern is operating, not that they experience it as theirs. A reader could reasonably say 'this speed is just how my job works, not something I do' — which is why Three lands on what they stopped waiting for rather than on a feeling, and Four asks them to claim one instance rather than to own the trait. The ask survives being wrong because naming one moment costs nothing and reveals something even if the read is off. The sentence that serves me more than them would be anything about 'unlocking potential' — cut.
